Q: Python format size application (converting B to KB, MB, GB, TB) A:

to avoid calling logarithm (math.log)
you can derive the exponent from len(bin(int(n)))

# binary-prefixed decimal units: B, KiB, MiB, GiB, ...
format_size=lambda n:((lambda L:f'{n/1024**L:.2f}{("KMGTPEZYRQ"[L-1]+"i")*(L>0)}'.rstrip("0").rstrip("."))((len(bin(int(n)))-1)//10))+"B"

or from len(str(int(n)))

# decimal units: B, KB, MB, GB, ...
format_size=lambda n:((lambda L:f'{n/1e3**L:.2f}{" KMGTPEZYRQ"[L]}'.rstrip('0').rstrip('.')if L else str(n))((len(str(int(n)))-1)//3))+"B"

Q: REST API fetches data very slow, how to make it fast? A:

The core problem is architectural, not a tuning issue

You're treating the external dataset as a live dependency on every request. The real fix is to decouple data sync from serving: pull the dataset into your own database once, then serve from there. This gives you full control over query performance and removes the external dependency from your hot path entirely.

Why in-memory / Redis is overkill here

The dataset is large (~271 MB JSON), cold-starts are expensive, and the data barely changes. Keeping 150k+ city records in Redis memory is wasteful and fragile — if the process restarts, you're back to a slow initial load. A proper indexed database is the right tool for infrequently-changing reference data.

Recommended architecture (two separate flows)

Flow 1 — data sync (runs on a schedule, completely separate from your API)

Set up a weekly cron or a one-time script that:

  1. Downloads the dataset from the GitHub releases page (CSV or MongoDB dump are the smallest formats — see the size table in their README)

  2. Parses and upserts into your own MongoDB collections: countries, states, cities

  3. Creates compound indexes:

// countries
db.countries.createIndex({ iso2: 1 })

// states
db.states.createIndex({ country_code: 1 })

// cities
db.cities.createIndex({ country_code: 1, state_id: 1 })

This sync job runs independently of your frontend traffic. Your API never touches the external dataset again.

Flow 2 — UI to backend

Don't send the full country list on load. Instead:

GET /api/locations?type=countries            → top 20 countries (by traffic/relevance)
GET /api/locations?type=countries&q=ger      → search, returns ≤20 matches
GET /api/locations?type=states&countryIso2=DE
GET /api/locations?type=cities&countryIso2=DE&stateId=123

The dropdown renders immediately with the top 20. A search input lets users find any country on demand — one indexed query, fast.
Cache the top-20 response client-side so navigating back to the dropdown doesn't re-fetch it from backend. For a more robust solution, React Query or SWR handle stale-while-revalidate automatically.

To answer your specific questions

  1. Best way to handle large JSON datasets: don't read from JSON files per-request; import once into a database with proper indexes.

  2. MongoDB vs Redis vs static files: MongoDB with indexes is the right choice here. Redis is for hot session data, not 150k-record reference tables. Static JSON files work but you lose query flexibility and incremental updates.

  3. Recommended architecture: exactly the two-flow design above — sync job decoupled from serving.

  4. Loading countries directly in the frontend: only the top-N preload should be in the frontend bundle; the full list should remain on-demand via the API. Shipping a 271 MB JSON to the client is not an option.

  5. Better dataset alternatives: the dr5hn dataset is excellent and is the de facto standard for this use case. The issue isn't the dataset — it's how you're consuming it.

Quick wins while you're setting this up

  • Add Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400 on your /api/locations?type=countries response — CDN or browser will cache the top-20 list for 24 hours

  • If you're on Nginx, make sure gzip on is enabled for JSON responses — the 250-country payload compresses ~85%

Q: How can I add a time to display an input button A:

Use setTimeout function:

setTimeout(function() { /*code here*/ }, 10000 /*time in milliseconds*/ );

Read more about it @ setTimeout : MDN

As a side note I recommended pure js because jQuery increases load on the server

Q: JavaScript img slider with fade A:

setTimeout is not what you need. First of all you must know that setTimeout function is not always precise. On your code the problem has to do with the one-thread, non-blocking nature of javascript. When you go into the loop of loopChange function what it really happens is:

the execution comes to the loop part. The variable i is instantiated having the value 0. The loop runs 10 times. During all this times each "setTimeout" call tells javascript "I know you can only run one thread. So, when you finish what you are doing change the opacity after i*200 milliseconds". Though, what javascript is doing is to iterate! So when the iteration ends then all these queued commands will execute.

And now we get in the asynchronous nature of the language. Exactly because all the commands will execute AFTER the iteration ends the variable i will have the value 10. So all of the setTimeout will execute:

changeOpacity((1-(10*0.02)))},(10*200)

This is why this code doesn't work. I believe that the jQuery animate proposed by TheOtherGuy is a good solution though I would consider working with css3 transitions which are much smoother. Take a look here: http://www.w3schools.com/css3/css3_transitions.asp

Q: Why does trying to call this external program from a Python script result in errors? A:

list2cmdline only adds quotes around an element if it contains spaces or tabs. So your three list elements get joined into roughly:

tageditor-cli "set cover=\"C:\Users\lords\...\Untitled Project 2.jpg\"" "-f \"C:\Users\...\Untitled Project 2.mp4\""

tageditor's argument parser treats -f as a flag that consumes following positional values as files. It also treats the bare path inside that first mashed-up arg as another positional file (because it contains a path-looking thing after parsing). That's where the error comes from.

Each CLI token must be its own list element. No combining set cover=... into one string, no combining -f "path" into one string, no manual quoting:

import os
import subprocess

export_path = r"C:\Users\lords\Videos\MCOC Videos"
file_prefix = "Untitled Project 2"

cover_path = os.path.join(export_path, f"{file_prefix}.jpg")
video_path = os.path.join(export_path, f"{file_prefix}.mp4")

cmd = [
    "tageditor-cli",
    "set",
    f"cover={cover_path}",   # no quotes — subprocess handles spaces
    "-f",
    video_path,              # no quotes
]

try:
    result = subprocess.run(
        cmd,
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        timeout=10,
        check=True,
    )
    print(result.stdout)
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    print("The command timed out.")
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
    print(f"Command failed with exit code {e.returncode}: {e.stderr}")
